doc.title: Ralph Sutton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995

title: Playing overseas and sitting in with unknown local musicians
summary: He enjoys warm audiences in Britain and Ireland and joins local players with no preparation.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: What was different, is there a difference playing overseas, with the audiences?

For me there is. I mean I enjoy that a lot, to play in England, Scotland. I just had a tour of England, Scotland and Ireland last month. But it seems like there’s a different sort of warm appreciation. They really make you feel good.
Great. When you go to those places, in recent years, who are your band mates that you like to—
Well no I join up with the guys wherever I go.

See that’s a concept that is really interesting I think to students. The idea of going across the seas and you don’t know who you’re going to play with. And the number of songs that you have to have at your disposal. I mean if you’re in Ireland for instance, what kinds of songs do you expect those musicians to be able to know?
No. Sometimes I’ll play solo when I go in, or this last trip in, not Belfast but the other one, okay, anyway—
That’s it. I played with they had two pianists this one night, two pianists. And a bass man and a drummer. So that’s how that worked out.
And you call a tune and hope they know it or they say—
No they’d say how about playing this? Okay. Or if you don’t know that, or maybe I don’t know it. You know so it’s not that hard. Everything falls into place.

But it’s still interesting, I think, for classical musicians too, to think how that works. I don’t know if a classical, if you got three classical musicians together, if they could play enough songs from memory. You know, shall we play a Haydn sonata, or—
They’d better bring the music for it.
They would probably bring the music, yeah.
